content.text: When the user switches away, your app isn't running in the background; it's waiting, and both Android and iOS may kill it to free memory without calling a single line of your code. The user doesn't know that and expects to come back to the same screen. Save what matters while the app is still in front, and let Flutter's state restoration rebuild the UI.

A user writes a long review in your food delivery app, switches to the camera to photograph the dish, answers a couple of messages and comes back. The app opens on its home screen and the review is gone. The bug report says "the app crashed", but your crash reporter shows nothing, because nothing crashed: the system ended the process while it sat in the background, and your code never found out.
The belief: when the user switches to another app, yours keeps running in the background until they close it, and before it goes away for good, it gets a chance to clean up:

It's a reasonable belief. Desktop apps work that way. The app switcher shows your app as if it were alive, and most of the time, when you come back quickly, it is: same screen, same scroll position. On a development phone with plenty of free memory, you may never see anything else. The half-truth: the process often survives a short trip away. The system just doesn't promise it, and it doesn't warn you when it changes its mind.
In the background, your app waits

Android's docs call it "an unusual and fundamental feature": an app process's lifetime "isn't directly controlled by the application itself". The system ranks processes by importance, and an app the user can't see falls to the bottom, into the cached list, where "the system is free to kill it as needed when resources like memory are needed elsewhere." A well-running system does this regularly; it isn't an emergency. Apple's docs ask a background app to do "as little work as possible, and preferably nothing", and Flutter's state restoration guide sums up both platforms: the OS "might kill the backgrounded app to release memory".
A process that's killed runs no more Dart code. Flutter's

docs say it plainly: apps "should not rely on always receiving all possible notifications", and if the app is killed by a kill signal, no notification is sent. Android says the same about its own callbacks:
"is not guaranteed to be called" when the system kills the process. So there's no
The user still expects their screen back

Android's guide on saving UI state separates two cases. If the user swipes the app away from Recents or force-stops it, they expect a clean start, and that's what they get. If they briefly switch to another app, "they expect to find the search keyword and results still there", even though "the system may destroy the application process while the user is away". Bridging that gap is your job, not the platform's.

blocks.title: Make process death happen on demand

content.text: Turn on "Don't keep activities" in Android's developer options, which destroys an activity as soon as the user leaves it, or press Home and run
with your package name, which kills only processes that are safe to kill. Then reopen the app from the launcher. Turn the option off when you're done.
